title: Chapter 11 Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of saving, loading, device handling, and model deployment!

questions.question: What is the recommended way to save a model's parameters for later inference?
questions.explanation: Saving the state_dict is the standard and most portable method.

questions.question: What must you do before loading a state_dict into a model?
options: Instantiate the model with the same architecture
questions.explanation: You need an instance of the exact same model class to receive the weights.

questions.question: `model.load_state_dict(torch.load('weights.pth'))` will automatically move the model to GPU if the weights were saved from a GPU model.
questions.explanation: You must handle device placement; use `map_location` to load onto a different device.

questions.question: To save a training checkpoint containing model, optimizer, and epoch, you typically create a ________ containing all these items and call `torch.save`.
questions.explanation: A Python dict is the standard way to bundle checkpoint components.

questions.question: What information does `optimizer.state_dict()` contain?
options: Momentum buffers and other optimizer-specific state
questions.explanation: It holds per‑parameter optimizer state like momentum, variance, etc.

questions.question: How do you move a model from GPU to CPU?
What does `nn.DataParallel` do?
options: Splits input batch across multiple GPUs, runs the same model on each
Moves the model to multiple CPUs
questions.explanation: It replicates the model on each GPU and divides the batch.

questions.question: A model wrapped with `nn.DataParallel` will have 'module.' prefix in its state_dict keys when saved.
questions.explanation: Yes, DataParallel adds a 'module' wrapper, so parameter names get that prefix.

questions.question: How can you load a GPU-trained state_dict on a CPU-only machine?
options: First move the file to CPU using scp
questions.explanation: `map_location='cpu'` remaps all tensors to CPU during load.

questions.question: What is the purpose of TorchScript?
options: To serialize and optimize models for production without Python dependency
questions.explanation: TorchScript creates a graph representation that can be run in C++.

questions.question: Which method records operations by running an example input?
questions.explanation: `trace` executes the model once and records the graph.

questions.question: When should you use `torch.jit.script` instead of `torch.jit.trace`?
options: When you need to save space
When the model contains data‑dependent control flow (if/for)
questions.explanation: Scripting can handle dynamic Python control flow that tracing cannot.

questions.question: What is ONNX?
options: An open format for representing machine learning models
questions.explanation: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) allows models to be shared across frameworks.

questions.question: How do you export a PyTorch model to ONNX?
questions.explanation: `torch.onnx.export` traces and exports the model to ONNX format.

questions.question: Which tool is PyTorch's native serving solution for deploying models as REST APIs?
questions.explanation: TorchServe is the official serving framework for PyTorch models.

questions.question: Quantization reduces model size and speeds up inference by using lower-precision arithmetic.
questions.explanation: Quantization (e.g., float32 -> int8) reduces memory and compute.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of `model.cpu()` over `model.to('cpu')`?
options: There is no advantage; they are equivalent
questions.explanation: `model.cpu()` is just a convenience wrapper for `model.to('cpu')`.

questions.question: If you have 4 GPUs and use `nn.DataParallel(model)`, how many copies of the model exist during forward pass?
questions.explanation: The model is replicated on each available GPU.

questions.question: What is a common use of `torch.jit.save`?
options: Save the model in TorchScript format for production
